paper_title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and reasoning about visual content in the digital world (Alayrac et al., 2022). Building upon these advances, recent efforts have begun to extend such capabilities beyond the digital realm into the physical world, positioning VLMs as key foundation for embodied AI (Driess et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). However, extending VLMs from the digital to the physical world requires more than semantic understanding: it demands geometrically grounded spatial intelligence for reasoning and acting in 3D environments. To extend VLMs beyond semantic understanding, recent studies have explored various ways to enhance their spatial reasoning capabilities. SpatialVLM (Chen et al., 2024) learns qualitative and quantitative spatial concepts from large-scale spatial question-answering data, while SpatialRGPT (Cheng et al., 2024) augments region-level representations with monocular depth cues for object-centric reasoning. 3D-LLM (Hong et al., 2023), in contrast, grounds language models in reconstructed 3D scene representations. Despite these advances, spatial benchmarks such as VSIBench reveal persistent limitations in current models ability to construct and reason about 3D space from visual observations (Yang et al., 2025). Moreover, the geometric information available to these models is typically inferred from monocular observations or supplied through estimated depth and reconstructed 3D representations, making it difficult to determine whether their spatial predictions are grounded in geometric evidence directly available from visual observations or primarily reflect learned priorsa concern reinforced by evidence-absent evaluations showing that VLMs can exploit sceneand category-level priors (Zhang et al., 2026). Calibrated stereo provides explicit geometric constraints for metric 3D perception: cross-view correspondences determine disparity, which can be converted into metric depth using known camera intrinsics and baseline. Yet, providing binocular observations alone does not guarantee that VLM will acquire geometric representations that generalize beyond the training distribution. Existing stereo methods primarily focus on geometric estimation, while VLMs typically treat paired images as generic visual inputs without explicitly learning the geometric relations between them. This raises central question: How can VLM learn transferable representations from binocular geometry that support metric 3D perception and high-level spatial reasoning? To investigate this question, we introduce StereoVLM, geometry-aware binocular VLM designed to learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated stereo observations. To connect binocular geometry with spatial understanding, we organize the training supervision into hierarchy of tasks spanning pixel-level correspondence, disparity estimation, calibration-conditioned metric depth, and object-level spatial reasoning. This hierarchy progressively connects cross-view matching to image-space geometric measurement and then to metric-scale estimation, before extending the learned geometry to language-referred objects and task-relevant 3D grounding. Importantly, we find that disparity provides substantially more generalizable supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, motivating its role as an intermediate geometric representation between cross-view correspondence and metric depth. We further establish Stereo3D-Bench to evaluate this progression across point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning. Beyond conventional task accuracy, controlled right-view interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation test whether model predictions genuinely depend on valid cross-view geometry. Compared with matched training without stereo instructions, hierarchical geometric supervision raises the five-benchmark spatial-reasoning average by 3.54 points and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) manipulation success by 4.3 percentage points. Our contributions are: We introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning, with hierarchical supervision that connects cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and language-grounded spatial reasoning, yielding transferable 3D spatial representations. We establish Stereo3D-Bench, comprehensive benchmark spanning point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning, together with verifiable evaluation protocol that uses controlled input interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation to test whether predictions genuinely rely on binocular geometry. 2 We demonstrate that disparity provides more generalizable geometric supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, while hierarchical geometric supervision benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Spatial reasoning in vision-language models Existing studies have enhanced spatial reasoning in VLMs through spatial instruction tuning (Chen et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2026), depth-aware visual representations (Cheng et al., 2024), and 3D grounding (Hong et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b). Meanwhile, benchmarks such as VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) reveal that current multimodal models still struggle with metric 3D understanding and spatial reasoning. Recent works explore metric depth prediction in VLMs, including queried-point prediction in DepthLM (Yeh et al., 2026) and dense prediction in DepthVLM (Yu et al., 2026). VLM3 (Cai et al., 2026) covers metric depth, cross-image correspondence, camera pose estimation, and object-level 3D understanding through separate task-specific training. Joint learning across low-level geometry and high-level semantic spatial understanding remains less explored. Stereo vision and embodied intelligence Stereo vision recovers scene geometry by establishing cross-view correspondence and converting disparity into depth using camera calibration. Modern stereo methods, including RAFT-Stereo (Lipson et al., 2021), IGEV-Stereo (Xu et al., 2023), FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and S2M2 (Min et al., 2025), employ correlation or geometry volumes to achieve accurate and generalizable disparity estimation. Recent work has begun incorporating binocular sensing into embodied systems. StereoVLA (Deng et al., 2025) fuses stereo-geometric and monocular-semantic features and adds auxiliary depth and camera-parameter objectives for VLA manipulation, while StereoPolicy (Han et al., 2026) uses cross-view attention to adapt diffusion policies and pretrained VLA policies without explicit 3D reconstruction. EATR-Stereo (Wu et al., 2026) further routes paired-view evidence according to proprioceptive state for long-horizon humanoid control, and VLBiMan (Zhou & Jia, 2026) combines vision-language grounding with calibrated stereo reconstruction in modular one-shot bimanual system. These methods demonstrate the value of binocular cues, with primary focus on geometric estimation or embodied action. Our work bridges embodied stereo sensing and VLM spatial reasoning through stereo VLM jointly trained on cross-view correspondence, disparity estimation, calibration-conditioned metric depth perception, and high-level semantic spatial reasoning.

sections.title: 3 STEREO3D-BENCH
sections.content: Stereo3D-Bench evaluates whether binocular evidence supporting metric geometry also transfers to language-grounded understanding of objects and task-relevant 3D structure. Its main split draws on four data sourcesDROID, Xperience-10M, FSD, and RoboCasaand covers all eight tasks. An out-of-domain (OOD) split uses independently collected in-house data to evaluate point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth. Figure 2 illustrates the benchmark construction and task hierarchy. Controlled right-view interventions further test whether predictions depend on valid cross-view correspondence rather than merely on the presence of second image. The supplementary material details data and question construction (section A), split and leakage controls (section B), and the evaluation protocol (section C). 3.1 TASK HIERARCHY Stereo3D-Bench comprises eight tasks across three levels: three point-level geometry tasks, three object-level geometry tasks, and two object-level spatial reasoning tasks. Each query is posed as short language question on an ordered stereo pair. Depending on the task, the model returns coordinate, scalar, 2D box, or an oriented 3D box with an object label. Point-level geometry. Given queried pixel in the left image, the model predicts its corresponding location in the right image, its horizontal disparity, or its metric depth along the left-camera optical axis. These tasks assess the models ability to establish cross-view correspondence, estimate binocular disparity, and recover metric scene geometry from stereo observations. Object-level geometry. The same three geometric tasks are applied to an object specified by language. Object correspondence returns its matching bounding box in the right image, object Figure 2: Construction and task hierarchy of Stereo3D-Bench. (a) The main split is constructed from four stereo data sources. Independently selected pointand object-level subsets contain 2,017 and 1,556 stereo pairs, respectively, yielding 94,546 questionanswer instances. (b) Representative queries and answer formats for eight tasks spanning point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning. disparity predicts its representative disparity, and object depth predicts its representative metric depth along the left-camera optical axis. Object-level spatial reasoning. Oriented 3D grounding identifies referred object and predicts its label and oriented 3D bounding box in the rectified-left camera frame. Task-target grounding instead receives manipulation instruction, identifies the object to be manipulated, and predicts that objects oriented 3D bounding box. Together, these tasks test whether model can progress from matching individual pixels, to associating geometry with named objects, and to grounding task-relevant objects in metric 3D space. 3.2 DATA SOURCES AND VQA CONSTRUCTION The main split combines real-world data from DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and Xperience10M (Ropedia, 2026) with synthetic data from FSD (Wen et al., 2025) and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024). For the synthetic sources, FSD provides rendered ground-truth disparity, while RoboCasa provides ground-truth disparity and depth directly from the simulator. FSD lacks physical metric calibration and is therefore evaluated only for correspondence and disparity. For the real-world sources, DROID provides aligned sensor depth, while Xperience-10M provides its officially released metric stereo-depth annotations. The five object-level tasks are evaluated on DROID and Xperience-10M. Evaluation data. The main split uses held-out samples from the four sources above. Training and evaluation data are separated before annotation generation. DROID is split by scene (laboratory, robot, and collection date), and Xperience-10M by recording UUID; all images and derived questions from held-out groups are excluded from training. FSD evaluation frames are excluded from training, while RoboCasa reserves five of its 24 task identities for evaluation and excludes all associated samples from training. We encode these targets as separate question-answer pairs and jointly optimize the model across all three question types. Correspondence supervision emphasizes cross-view localization, disparity supervision quantifies image-space displacement, and depth supervision requires interpreting that displacement under the supplied calibration. Deriving all three targets from common geometric reference preserves their geometric relationship during target construction, while joint training encourages the model to learn both cross-view matching and its connection to metric scale. Language-grounded object supervision. Point-level supervision captures local stereo geometry. To associate this geometry with semantic entities and their spatial extent, we introduce objectlevel supervision conditioned on linguistic references. Object correspondence, disparity, and depth link the referred object to its cross-view location and geometric measurements, while oriented 3D grounding supervises its position, dimensions, and orientation in the rectified-left camera frame. Task-target grounding further requires the model to identify and localize the object specified by manipulation instruction. Together, these objectives extend supervision from local geometric estimation to language-conditioned object localization and task-relevant 3D grounding. 4.3 JOINT TRAINING OBJECTIVE We jointly optimize StereoVLM over point-level geometry, object-level grounding, and general multimodal instructions. All tasks share the conditional answer-generation formulation in section 4.1, 6 allowing geometric measurements and language-grounded spatial outputs to be learned under unified objective. sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Model and training setup. We initialize StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B from the corresponding Qwen3-VL-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) checkpoints. Unless otherwise specified, our final models are instruction-tuned for 3,000 steps with all parameters updated, using an initial learning rate of 1105, warmup ratio of 0.03, and an effective global batch size of 64. Stereo images are processed at resolution of 800 320. Stereo instructions account for 25% of the sampled training mixture, with 15% assigned to point-level geometry and 10% to object-level supervision. The remaining 75% comprises general visual-language, grounding, spatial-reasoning, tracking, and robotics instructions. Full data and optimization details are provided in section D.1. Evaluation. We evaluate StereoVLM on Stereo3D-Bench for binocular geometry and object-level spatial understanding, on five external benchmarks (Omni3D (Brazil et al., 2023), DA-2K (Yang et al., 2024), OmniSpatial (Jia et al., 2026), MindCube (Wang et al., 2025a), and VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025)) for spatial-reasoning transfer, and on RoboCasa for manipulation performance. We further assess geometric generalization on the independently collected in-house OOD split of Stereo3DBench, focusing on point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth. Evaluation splits are described in section B. Settings specific to each experiment are provided in the corresponding subsections. 5.2 LEARNING TRANSFERABLE BINOCULAR REPRESENTATIONS We analyze how the choice of geometric supervision affects metric-depth generalization. We compare monocular depth, binocular depth, and binocular disparity under controlled geometry-only setting. We then analyze whether joint disparitydepth training learns the calibrated conversion between the two quantities and whether geometric supervision benefits object-level spatial understanding. Which geometric supervision generalizes better? We initialize all three variants from the same Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct checkpoint and train them exclusively on geometry QA constructed from the same 234K rectified stereo pairs, using an identical optimization budget. The monocular-depth variant receives only the left image and directly predicts metric depth. The binocular-depth variant receives the ordered stereo pair and camera calibration and also predicts depth directly. The binoculardisparity variant predicts horizontal disparity from the ordered pair; at evaluation, depth is recovered using calibration via eq. (5). We follow each baselines official preprocessing and inference settings, including its model-specific input resolution. Before scoring, predicted image coordinates and disparities expressed on the width-1000 normalized scale are converted to pixels at the benchmark image resolution. Results are reported only for tasks supported by each model. Point-level geometry. StereoVLM-8B achieves the best results across all three point-level tasks in Table 4. Under the same stereo-input protocol, it reduces correspondence MAE from 9.27 to 3.80 pixels and disparity MAE from 7.55 to 3.76 pixels relative to GPT-6 Astra, while increasing depth δ1 from 75.96% to 95.17%. StereoVLM-2B also surpasses GPT-6 Astra on all three tasks, reaching 94.51% in depth δ1. The remaining general-purpose VLMs exhibit substantially weaker stereo geometric performance, whereas the depth-specialized baselines receive only the left image and do not exploit binocular evidence in this evaluation. Compared with the single-view DepthVLM-4B reference, StereoVLM-8B improves depth δ1 by 58.06 percentage points. Together, these results show consistent improvements in image-space geometry and metric-depth estimation across both model scales. Language-grounded 3D reasoning. Across the five object-level tasks, StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B achieve average scores of 64.43% and 66.98%, outperforming GPT-6 Astra by 16.82 and 19.37 percentage points, respectively. The advantage is particularly pronounced in 3D localization: StereoVLM-8B increases oriented 3D-box mIoU from 17.92% to 37.70% and target Joint@0.25 from 12.82% to 51.28%. Both variants also surpass the single-view DepthVLM-4B reference, which achieves an object-level average of 14.35%. Scaling from 2B to 8B improves all five object-level metrics. These results demonstrate stronger 3D grounding of language-referred objects and task targets, complementing the gains in point-level geometry. sections.title: 5.4 TRANSFER BEYOND STEREO3D-BENCH
sections.content: We test spatial reasoning and embodied control using matched 2B models trained with and without stereo instructions. Both share the same initialization, optimization schedule, and training budget. Removing stereo instructions preserves the relative sampling proportions of the remaining categories. General spatial reasoning. We evaluate general spatial reasoning on three monocular benchmarks (Omni3D, DA-2K, and OmniSpatial) and two video benchmarks (MindCube and VSI-Bench). Table 6 shows that adding stereo instructions improves all five benchmarks, increasing the overall average from 47.94 to 51.48, gain of 3.54 percentage points. The largest gain occurs on Omni3D at 8.21 points, while the video benchmarks MindCube and VSI-Bench improve by 3.71 and 0.92 points, respectively. With shared spatial supervision, correct stereo and single-left training yield similar averages (50.23 and 50.21). Adding correspondence and disparity supervision to correct stereo raises the average to 51.48 (section D.6.1). Embodied control. We further evaluate whether the learned representation benefits downstream robotic control. We initialize the same GR00T policy (Bjorck et al., 2025) architecture from the pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B model and representation models trained with and without stereo instructions. Each policy is trained for 60k steps using 50 demonstrations per task and evaluated on 24 RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) tasks with 50 rollouts per task. To isolate the benefit of stereo supervision from exposure to RoboCasa data during representation training, we exclude RoboCasa from the representation-training mixture for this embodied-control experiment. Table 7 shows that stereo instruction tuning increases manipulation success from 38.1% to 42.4%, gain of 4.3 percentage points over general instruction tuning alone. It also exceeds the pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B initialization at 34.9% by 7.5 points. All policies share the same stereo-input setting and downstream training protocol. Further controls support the benefits of geometric supervision and valid binocular observations for manipulation (section D.6.2).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: We present StereoVLM, geometry-aware binocular vision-language model for metric 3D spatial reasoning, trained with hierarchical stereo supervision from cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and semantic spatial reasoning. We show that disparity supervision provides substantially stronger metric-depth generalization to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision, while controlled interventions verify that StereoVLM benefits from valid cross-view geometry. Hierarchical geometric supervision further benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control. The current study is limited by its focus on controlled benchmarks and simulated kitchen tasks, as well as its reliance on calibrated and synchronized cameras; future work should address the simulation-to-real gap and improve robustness to challenging visual conditions and diverse robot platforms.

sections.title: SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL
sections.content: This supplementary material documents the construction and evaluation of Stereo3D-Bench, together with additional training details and experiments for StereoVLM. Training and benchmark pairs follow shared processing and annotation procedure but are kept separate by the data split. The sections below describe this procedure, the split, the evaluation protocol, and supporting results. section A: Geometric references, semantic annotations, and query and answer schemas, with point-level and object-level examples. section B: The training mixture, the main and OOD splits of Stereo3D-Bench, and per-source counts for the main split. section C: Metric definitions, invalid outputs, and the implementation of right-view interventions. section D: Training settings, geometric generalization, input controls, extrinsic robustness, baseline sensitivity, transfer experiments, and modular stereoVLM comparisons.

sections.content: Training data and Stereo3D-Bench share the same stereo representation, question schemas, and coordinate conventions, but intentionally use different geometric-reference pathways. Training supervision uses FoundationStereo predictions, whereas Stereo3D-Bench is scored against source-native geometric references. This separation prevents benchmark performance from directly measuring reproduction of the stereo estimator used to construct the training data. The following subsections describe the shared representation, the training and evaluation reference pathways, the semantic annotations, and question generation. Dataset splitting and leakage control are described in section B. During preprocessing, camera intrinsics are standardized across calibrated stereo datasets. Disparity is expressed in rectified-left pixel coordinates, and physical depth is represented by the left-camera optical-axis distance in meters. Training and evaluation pairs use the same representation but differ in reference provenance. FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) provides dense disparity supervision for the training mixture. In Stereo3D-Bench, DROID uses its aligned sensor depth, Xperience-10M uses its officially released stereo-depth annotation, RoboCasa uses simulator geometry, and FSD uses its source-native disparity reference. Because FSD does not provide physical metric calibration, it contributes correspondence and disparity questions but not metric-depth questions. Four diagnostic conditions alter the availability or validity of the right view. Single-left input removes the second image, (Il). Duplicated-left input places the left image in both slots, (Il, Il). Zero-right input replaces the right view with an equally sized black image, (Il, 0). Shuffled-right input replaces the correct right image with right image from another benchmark example, (Il, r). Scores under these four conditions are reported separately and do not enter the primary Stereo3D-Bench score.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL RESULTS
sections.content: This section provides the training-data composition and optimization settings omitted from the main paper, followed by geometric generalization evaluation and additional analyses of the single-view 19 capability retained after stereo training, robustness to extrinsic calibration errors, sensitivity to the supplied baseline, and transfer to spatial reasoning and embodied control. We also provide qualitative results and compare modular stereoVLM pipelines. D.1 TRAINING DATA AND OPTIMIZATION Stereo training data. We construct the stereo instruction data from DROID, FSD, Xperience10M, and RoboCasa. RoboCasa contributes point-level geometry instructions. All stereo pairs are processed using the construction procedure in section A. Table 10 reports the training inventory after filtering and data expansion. Geometry and semantic pairs are counted separately because the two annotation pipelines retain different subsets of the source images. Geometry QA counts denote complete questionanswer records rather than individual points within multi-point question. Semantic counts cover the five object-level task families used in the final model and benchmark. Geometry-only training data. The three geometry-only variants compared in table 1 are trained on the same 234K rectified stereo pairs from Xperience-10M, DROID, RoboCasa, and an in-house training collection. Instruction mixture. Stereo instructions account for 25% of the final instruction mixture. We allocate 15% to point-level stereo geometry and 10% to object-level stereo semantics, preserving 60:40 ratio within the stereo portion. The remaining 75% is distributed among the monocular and video instruction categories in proportion to their previous weights. The resulting top-level sampling probabilities are shown in fig. 8. These probabilities specify the composition of the instruction stream after construction of the stereo inventory above. Table 10: Stereo training inventory. We initialize each StereoVLM variant from the corresponding Qwen3-VL-Instruct checkpoint and perform full-parameter instruction tuning, including the vision encoder, language model, and multimodal aligner. The final 2B and 8B models share the same training data mixture and optimization schedule. Both are trained for 3,000 optimization steps with an initial learning rate of 1 105, warmup ratio of 0.03, and an effective global batch size of 64. We use maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens, bfloat16 computation, gradient checkpointing, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2. Stereo images are presented at 800 320, the same resolution used to construct the geometric and semantic references. Dataset and training-order shuffling use fixed random seed. The reduced-supervision input controls are described separately in section D.6. 20 D.2 GEOMETRIC GENERALIZATION TO UNSEEN SCENES We further evaluate geometric generalization on the in-house OOD split of Stereo3D-Bench. Table 11 reports point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth results using the same metrics as the main split. D.3 SINGLE-VIEW CAPABILITY AND INPUT CONTROLS Although StereoVLM is trained with explicit stereo supervision, it is not restricted to binocular inputs. Prior work examines how selfsupervised monocular depth estimators generalize across domains (Yao et al., 2024). To evaluate the monocular capability retained by the model after stereo instruction tuning, we remove the right image and provide only the rectified left image. We also remove the stereo baseline from the question. The checkpoint, focal length, remaining question text, and decoding configuration are otherwise unchanged. This setting prevents the model from using binocular correspondence and measures what can be recovered from monocular appearance, object-scale priors, and pretrained visual-language knowledge. StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B obtain point-level depth δ1 scores of 73.51 and 63.22, respectively, compared with 43.88 for the strongest general-purpose baseline. StereoVLM-2B also reaches an object-depth δ1 of 81.52. For oriented 3D grounding, StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B achieve mIoU scores of 16.92 and 6.82, respectively. On task-target grounding, their Joint@0.25 scores are 25.64 and 28.21, respectively, exceeding the strongest general-purpose baseline at 7.69. Compared with the stereo-input results in table 4, GPT-6 Astras point-level depth δ1 drops from 75.96% to 43.88%, while its object-depth δ1 falls from 93.40% to 37.37%  (table 12)  . These correspond to decreases of 32.08 and 56.03 percentage points, respectively, indicating substantially higher depth accuracy under the stereo evaluation setting. These results suggest that GPT-6 Astra benefits from stereo conditioning for both point-level and object-level depth estimation, with more pronounced decline in object-depth accuracy under single-view input. These results indicate that stereo-representation training does not replace the monocular cues inherited from the pretrained model. Instead, StereoVLM remains usable when only one image is available, while the primary stereo evaluation measures the additional capability obtained from valid leftright pair. D.4 ROBUSTNESS TO EXTRINSIC CALIBRATION ERRORS Camera pose determines how 3D scene points project into an image (Yan et al., 2024; Yan & Xu, 2026). We test how sensitive StereoVLM is to small errors in the relative pose of the stereo cameras. Starting from rectified pair, we keep the left image, query pixels, nominal focal length, nominal baseline, and left-view depth references fixed, and perturb only the pose of the right camera. The resulting right image is rendered under one of six single-axis perturbations: rotations Rx, Ry, and Rz, or translations tx, ty, and tz. The experiment therefore measures sensitivity to imperfect stereo alignment without changing the scene or the queried left-view geometry. The evaluation contains 400 base pairs, comprising 200 DROID pairs and 200 in-house robot pairs. Each pair contributes eight fixed left-image query points. For every axis, we construct three perturbation levels, giving 3,200 queried points per axis and level. All three share reduced supervision set covering depth estimation, object-level and task-target 3D grounding, and other spatial tasks. Correspondence and disparity questions are excluded from this shared set because Single Left lacks the required right-view observation. StereoVLM uses correctly paired images and additionally includes correspondence and disparity supervision. Although only the rectified left image is shown for readability, both models receive the complete rectified leftright pair when producing each prediction. The three row groups correspond to object metric depth, semantic oriented 3D grounding, and task-target grounding. In these examples, both model scales recover object depth closely and produce 3D boxes with similar centers, extents, and orientations to the references. Only the left-view visualization is displayed; predictions are produced from the complete stereo pair. 28 D.8 COMPARISON WITH MODULAR STEREOVLM PIPELINES We evaluate whether general-purpose VLM equipped with an external stereo estimator can achieve comparable object-level spatial reasoning to StereoVLM. We construct two modular baselines using FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and frozen Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), and compare their semantic accuracy and end-to-end inference latency with StereoVLM-2B. Baseline construction. The two baselines differ in how stereo geometry is provided to the VLM. The localization-based pipeline first queries the VLM to localize the referred object in the left image. It then aggregates FoundationStereo-predicted disparities within the localized region using fixed central-window median and disparity-based filtering. The selected pixels are back-projected into 3D, and PCA-based heuristic estimates an approximate oriented bounding box of the visible surface. These geometric measurements are then provided to the VLM to generate the final answer. The direct-input pipeline instead provides the stereo RGB pair, predicted depth visualization, an 8 20 disparity/depth grid, and camera calibration to the VLM in single call. Neither baseline receives ground-truth answers, bounding boxes, or masks at inference time. StereoVLM-2B directly answers each question from the stereo RGB pair and the task prompt, including the applicable camera calibration, in one VLM call.
